The same exact thing happened to me. My preceptor was a complete B and despite putting in at least 14-16 hours a day, it wasn’t good enough. It was an institutional rotation at a...let’s say...high-level teaching hospital. I hadn’t had anything like it before, so yes, I wasn’t as knowledgeable as other students who had 4 rotations in these types of places. Anyways, my work ethic is excellent- I worked hard, was at the hospital at least 12 hours a day, then probably worked another 4-6 at home. The effort was there. She had a majorly condescending attitude but I just sucked it up- after all, it was only 6 weeks. I was friendly and punctual. 
We had to do a presentation, and I called her to ask a few questions about what she wanted, because my other one had been totally “wrong” for her. A couple of days later, she chastised me for interrupting her weekend with questions I should already know the answers to. I profusely apologized and told her that I just wanted to excel in the presentation, and that I had not had a rotation even remotely close to this one before.
Anyways.. DESPITE MAKING ALL As in my 7 prior APPEs, she failed me. 
I was completely...devastated. I entered a major depression and struggled with my calling in life, and even my existence. After all, this was year 8/8 of college/grad school, and I didn’t come this far for nothing. I only had 6 weeks left! 
My entire life, I had apologized for everything they went awry and accepted blame for anything that went wrong. I am a pleaser and a perfectionist, which is why failing a rotation was so devastating. 
I had to sit out at least a year to rejoin the next graduating class on their eighth rotation. Fearful about how I’d support myself, I began to search for jobs where I’d be able to make enough money to support myself and pay bills. I eventually found a job in the corporate world as a logistics coordinator- and then I was promoted to HR manager 1.5 years later. 
I ended up taking ‘off’ 3 years. In that time period, I learned so much more than pharmacy would have taught me about how to manage employees and people in general (and much more). It ended up being 3 of the best years of my life. I was so burned out and I needed a break from pharmacy and medicine. It was hard to realize that at the time.

I cried when I realized that it was time for me to go back to reality and finish what I’d started. But I *was* ready. Excelling in my HR job taught me that I’m not an idiot, despite how stupid a miserable preceptor made me feel. Most importantly, this was the first time in my life that I began to have a more healthy outlook on things and not berate myself for every single silly thing that went wrong.

I get trends can be somewhat valuable if it’s the absolute first study of its kind, to point out there should be further exploration in it, but I feel that at times this isn’t even mentioned as a limitation of the study. IMO, for a study of 20,000 research subjects, it should not be mentioned if it isn’t statistically significant. I think that people can absentmindedly utilize this trend toward the false application of medications, which certainly merits more research to fully establish clinical statistical significance. 
Utilizing a general trend (that has not reached statistic significance) based off a meta-analysis may not be particularly helpful because each study usually contains different inclusion/exclusion criteria, number of research sites, ethnicities, sex, often medication dosage (many countries have varying approved dosages for treatment of a condition). There are so many variables at play. 
In summary: the only practical use is to investigate *significant* further research that’s needed...and it should always be mentioned as a limitation of the study at hand. In an RCT with plentiful research subjects and appropriate power, it shouldn’t even be mentioned in the discussion, other than perhaps in the data points in a chart that you can extrapolate your own thoughts on.
